claims.text: The mammalian heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria above, which receive blood, and two thick-walled ventricles below, which pump it out. Four major vessels join it: the vena cava brings deoxygenated blood into the right atrium, the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium, and the aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

claims.text: The coronary arteries are narrow vessels that branch from the aorta close to its base and run over the outer surface of the heart, supplying the cardiac muscle of the heart wall with oxygenated blood. They are separate from the major vessels that leave the heart, the aorta and the pulmonary artery.

claims.text: Inside the heart a muscular septum separates the right side from the left, so deoxygenated and oxygenated blood do not mix. Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid on the left) lie between each atrium and ventricle; their flaps are held by valve tendons fixed to papillary muscles on the ventricle wall. Semilunar valves, each with three pocket-shaped cups, lie at the bases of the aorta and the pulmonary artery. The valves keep blood moving in one direction.

claims.text: The walls of the atria are thin because an atrium pushes blood only a short distance into the ventricle below it and the pressure needed is low, about 1 kPa; the walls of the ventricles are thick because the cardiac muscle must contract forcefully enough to raise the pressure of the blood above the pressure in the artery it leads into.

claims.text: The wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle because the left ventricle drives blood around the whole body at a high pressure (peak about 16 kPa in our values), whereas the right ventricle drives the same volume per beat through the nearby lungs at a much lower pressure (peak about 3 kPa in our values); a higher pressure in the thin-walled lung capillaries would risk damaging them.

claims.text: In one cardiac cycle the atria contract (atrial systole), pushing the last of their blood into the ventricles; the ventricles then contract (ventricular systole), forcing blood out into the aorta and the pulmonary artery; then the whole heart relaxes (diastole) and the atria fill with blood from the veins, which also flows on into the ventricles. Systole means contraction and diastole means relaxation.

claims.text: A layer of fibrous tissue between the atria and the ventricles does not conduct the wave of excitation, so the wave reaches the ventricles through the atrioventricular node (AVN) at the base of the atria, the one route across; the AVN delays the wave by about 0.1 s before passing it on, which lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.

claims.text: From the AVN the wave passes into the Purkyne tissue, which runs down the septum to the apex and then up through the ventricle walls; it conducts the wave quickly, so the ventricles contract from the apex upwards and blood is forced towards the arteries.
